svg.aria-label: Diagram: A CloudWatch alarm has three states. OK is a judgement that the metric is within threshold, ALARM is a judgement that it is breaching, and INSUFFICIENT_DATA is the absence of a judgement rather than a verdict of health. Four treatments decide what absent datapoints mean. notBreaching treats them as good and within the threshold, yielding OK and reporting health the alarm cannot see. breaching treats them as bad, yielding ALARM. ignore maintains whatever state the alarm already had. missing, which is the default behavior, transitions the alarm to INSUFFICIENT_DATA when all data points in the evaluation range are missing, so it fires no ALARM action. That default matters because an FIS stop condition is a CloudWatch alarm, so an experiment that broke the thing producing the metric can silence its own guardrail. One namespace overrides the global default: alarms on AWS/DynamoDB metrics default to ignore. The evaluation range is wider than the evaluation periods, because CloudWatch attempts to retrieve more data points than the Evaluation Periods setting, so an alarm with Evaluation Periods and Datapoints to Alarm both set to three retrieves the five most recent points, two more than it needs, and when enough real data points exist the missing-data treatment is not needed and is ignored, which means the setting only engages when data is genuinely sparse. Three further behaviours surprise readers. After a metric stops flowing CloudWatch may repeatedly re-evaluate the last set of data points, which can change state and re-execute actions. An alarm always enters ALARM when the oldest available breaching datapoint within the Evaluation Periods is at least as old as Datapoints to Alarm, even when fewer datapoints than M are available. And for Metrics Insights alarms across multiple series, a series no longer returned by the query transitions to OK regardless of the missing-data treatment, with a StateReason of no data was returned for this contributor, while an empty result at alarm level does apply the treatment. Separately, CloudWatch does not test or validate the actions specified on an alarm, nor detect errors from invoking nonexistent actions, so an alarm can evaluate and transition correctly and deliver nothing with no error recorded anywhere. Action semantics differ by type: actions fire only on state change, except Auto Scaling actions which repeat once per minute while the alarm stays in the new state, and composite alarms can notify but cannot perform EC2 or Auto Scaling actions. Alarm history is kept for 30 days.
svg.title: Not in ALARM is two states, and one of them is unknown
svg.text: Three states. The default sends a dead metric to the one that fires nothing.
“This might indicate that your resource is inactive, and might not necessarily mean that there is a problem.”
Four treatments for absent data — and what each says when it is all gone
missing (DEFAULT) → INSUFFICIENT_DATA fires no ALARM action at all
breaching → ALARM “treated as ‘bad’”
notBreaching → OK reports health it cannot see
ignore → whatever it was “current alarm state is maintained”
Why the default matters: #109’s guardrail is one of these alarms
An experiment that broke the thing producing the metric has silenced its own stop condition, and the
experiment runs on. INSUFFICIENT_DATA is the absence of a judgement, not a judgement of health.
And nothing checks the other end of the chain
“CloudWatch doesn’t test or validate the actions that you specify, nor does it detect any … errors
resulting from an attempt to invoke nonexistent actions.” A correct alarm can deliver nothing, silently.
The range is wider than the periods
CloudWatch retrieves “a higher number of data
points than … Evaluation Periods” — 5 for a
3-of-3 alarm, two spare.
With enough real points the treatment “is ignored”.
Two semantics, one alarm object
Actions fire “only when the alarm changes state”
— except Auto Scaling, “once per minute that the
alarm remains in the new state”.
Composites notify; they cannot scale or stop.
Three behaviours that catch people
metric stops re-evaluation “might cause the alarm to … re-execute actions”
M out of N enters ALARM “even if … datapoints available is lower than M”
series vanishes → OK “no matter the treat missing data treatment”
Before trusting a green alarm, establish that it can go red — and that something would hear it.
SetAlarmState forces any state and reverts at the next evaluation, so the end-to-end test is cheap. An alarm
nobody has seen fire is an alarm whose action has never been proven — the common case for the ones that matter.
